[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — uh — appreciate you taking the time. Quick intro: I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood hosted API side. With me today is Diego, our SE, and Ruth from product, she'll jump in on Optimize. Can we do quick intros from Nimble?
[00:07] Evan: Evan Li, engineering lead. We're looking to add chat-based claim triage, latency matters, cost matters.
[00:11] Priya: Priya, ML Eng. I'll be running the pilot and lookin' at model quality and perf.
[00:14] Sam: Sam, CTO. Mainly listening for infra and timelines.
[00:17] Jordan: Jordan, security — SOC2 and KMS questions later.
[00:20] Maya: Great. We'll run through a short quickstart — live call to hosted chat — show streaming and a couple ways to handle retries and then jump into the Console and Optimize recommendations.

[02:15] Diego: Alright I'm sharing my screen. First simple chat example: single HTTP POST to /v1/chat with API key. We start with a base system prompt, user messages, set temperature=0.2, max_tokens=256. The key bit is streaming: we open the response as a chunked stream, we get delta tokens. That lets UI show progressive results and lowers perceived latency.
[02:45] Evan: With streaming are you sending partial tokens more frequently? I'm worried about lots of small packets.
[02:51] Diego: Good question. The runtime batches tokens and partially aggregates; network chunk frequency is influenced by model tokenization and your client buffer. On Redwood we have streaming flush heuristics to avoid tiny‑packet spam and you can tune the stream delta size on the client.
[03:22] Priya: Do you recommend a single streaming connection per user, or multiplex? We have mobile clients.
[03:28] Diego: For mobile, one active stream per user session works best. For very chatty apps, multiplexing via a gateway is fine but watch concurrency limits.
[04:05] Ruth: Quick note from Optimize — we can surface batching suggestions based on your traffic pattern and suggest quantized model variants to cut token cost by 20–40% with small latency tradeoff.

[06:00] Diego: Now retries. Pattern we recommend: idempotency key per request, exponential backoff with jitter, and detect partial responses. If the client receives a truncated stream, you can either re-issue with same idempotency key and Redwood will resume or return consistent error codes.
[06:35] Sam: Resume? How does 'resume' work across streaming? If someone lost connection, will the model re-send the same continuation or can it produce a slightly different tail?
[06:47] Diego: It's a deterministic resume on the same model/version if you pin the model version. If you allow model rollouts to move, there could be slight diffs. Best practice: for resumability, pin model_version in the request and include the last token offset — Redwood will attempt KV cache resume where supported.

[08:10] Evan: What about multi-region fallback — if our primary region has a transient issue, can requests be routed to a secondary region?
[08:18] Maya: Yes, Smart Routing policy allows region fallback. We expose routing controls by customer tier and latency vs cost preference. For hosted customers we automatically fallback to compatible variants in seconds.

[10:04] Jordan: On security, do you store request payloads? What's retention and encryption?
[10:11] Maya: Hosted retention defaults to 30 days for telemetry, you can opt-out or configure retention. All data at rest is encrypted; for Private deployments you bring your own KMS/HSM. We'll share the security pack with SOC2, ISO docs — that was one of the next steps.

[12:22] Diego: Back to runtime failover — quick demo: I trigger a simulated pod drain, watch Console show an uptick in 5xxs then automatic fallback to a lower-cost model variant and a region — there's a graceful degradation policy that can trade cost for latency vs failing hard.
[12:45] Evan: Can we define a policy to prefer failing over cost increase? We need small teams watching our burn.
[12:51] Diego: Absolutely, that's a routing policy in the Console. You can set a priority order: e.g., try low-latency variants, then low-cost, or prefer failing fast. Policies are per-route and you can set SLO thresholds.

[15:00] Priya: For our pilot, we'd want a canary: send 5% traffic to a new quantized variant and compare quality. Does Console give diffs?
[15:08] Ruth: Yes, Optimize has a quality diff panel connected to prompt sets — it will run evaluations across example prompts and surface regression alerts. You can attach a prompt set, run batch eval, and see token-level deltas.

[17:10] Sam: How does billing work for streaming partials? Do you pay for partial tokens sent and then resumed tokens double billed?
[17:18] Maya: Billing is per-token consumed by the model. If a stream truncates and you resume, the runtime continues the token budget from the last committed token; duplicate retransmits at the network layer are not double-billed. We also show token-level charge breakdown in Console for per-route visibility.

[19:30] Evan: Are there SDKs for our stack? We're node backend + React Native frontends.
[19:36] Diego: Yes, official SDKs (node, python, go) and a lightweight JS client for streaming. For RN we recommend using the native websocket layer with our small client wrapper.

[22:02] Jordan: KMS: we want envelope encryption and customer-managed keys. How mature is that in hosted?
[22:09] Maya: Hosted supports bring-your-own-KMS for encryption at rest for enterprise customers; we do envelope encryption. For full private key control you can opt for Private deployment. We'll attach the KMS integration guide.

[24:15] Priya: For the pilot: expected qps ~30 during office hours, median utterance length ~50 tokens, peak 120 tokens. We want 99th percentile latency under 400ms. Does Redwood have published perf numbers?
[24:28] Diego: We have perf profiles in the model catalog. For chat workloads with that size, pinning to a lower-latency variant and enabling prefix caching for repeated system prompts should keep you under 400ms p99 in most regions. We'll run a quick benchmark in the lab with your exact prompt distribution.

[26:55] Evan: On caching — you mentioned KV cache, is that the decoder KV cache for generation or a separate prefix cache?
[27:02] Diego: Two caches: KV cache used internally to accelerate autoregressive generation between tokens; prefix/KV caching refers to caching repeated prompt prefixes so you avoid recomputing the same attention for identical system messages across requests. Prefix caching can drastically reduce cost for repetitive prompts.

[29:40] Priya: Any gotchas with prefix caching and personalization? We do per-user system prompts.
[29:46] Diego: If prompts vary per user you won't get much prefix cache hit. However, you can split static system instructions from dynamic user context, cache the static part and then append dynamic tokens at request time — that gives a good tradeoff.

[31:10] Ruth: Also Optimize will recommend split strategies and simulate expected cache hit rates based on your sample traffic.

[33:00] Maya: Let's walk a small failover sequence: client opens stream, network blips, stream truncated, client retries with same idempotency key and model_version pinned. Redwood resumes from last committed token; Console trace shows a resumed call and marks it as resume.
[33:28] Sam: What if the resume fails because the model variant changed mid-flight?
[33:33] Diego: If model_version mismatches, resume fails; Redwood will return a clear error code and depending on policy, you can either re-issue without pinning (accepting minor variance) or fail back to stored partial response.

[35:15] Jordan: Audit logs — can we get token-level audit trails for compliance? We need to show who invoked what model and when.
[35:23] Maya: Yes, per-request audit logs with token counts, model id, user id, and IP. For sensitive industries we recommend Private with longer retention. We'll include the audit log schema in the security packet.

[37:40] Evan: Ok cost math — assume 100k tokens/day; what's the ballpark?
[37:45] Maya: Depends on model variant and quantization. In hosted, we have per-token price tiers; Optimize will estimate monthly spend given your traffic. We'll send two scenarios in the pricing sheet: hosted standard and hosted with recommended quantized model.

[39:50] Priya: Is the Console able to show cost per route and per-token median latency in real time?
[39:57] Ruth: Yes, routing dashboards show token cost, latency percentiles, and model-level traces. You can slice by route, API key, or user id (if you forward that metadata).

[41:22] Diego: Demo wrap: I'm going to kick a small sandbox test — sending 50 parallel chat requests with small prompts to show console traces and fallback behavior.
[41:32] [screen demo noise: console traces, charts animating, a few 503 spikes simulated]
[43:00] Priya: That trace view is really useful — can we export raw traces for our SREs?
[43:06] Diego: Yes, there's an export button and API to pull raw trace logs.

[44:40] Jordan: Last question — compliance for EU data residency? We need data stored in EU.
[44:47] Maya: Hosted offers region-specific deployments and data residency options; for strict legal obligations we recommend a Private deployment in your VPC or our EU-hosted private plane. We'll outline the options in the security doc.

Jordan to confirm KMS questions and desired retention. Anything else?
